title: A Cry Against Surrounding Enemies
overview: A poet begs God to break his silence as a ring of neighboring nations plots to wipe Israel off the map, and asks God to defeat them as he did enemies in the past.

parts.label: Do not stay silent (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: The poet pleads with God to speak up and act, because enemies are openly plotting to destroy Israel so completely that even its name is forgotten. He treats an attack on God's people as an attack on God himself.

parts.label: A ring of nations (vv. 5-8)
parts.note: The list names peoples on every side of Israel: Edom, Moab and Ammon to the south and east, desert tribes, Philistia on the coast, Byblos and Tyre to the north, with distant Assyria backing Moab and Ammon, the 'descendants of Lot'. No single known event matches this exact list, so some link it to an invasion in King Jehoshaphat's time while others see it as a picture of all Israel's neighbors at once.

parts.label: Do it again (vv. 9-12)
parts.note: The poet recalls two old victories from Israel's stories: Deborah and Barak's defeat of the general Sisera and King Jabin by the Kishon river, and Gideon's rout of Midian and its leaders Oreb, Zeeb, Zebah and Zalmunna. He asks God to repeat those victories against the people who want to seize the land as their own.

parts.label: Wind, fire and storm (vv. 13-16)
parts.note: Images of tumbleweed, chaff blown off the threshing floor, wildfire and storm all picture enemies scattered and helpless. Yet verse 16 adds a hope that their shame might lead them to seek the LORD.

parts.label: That they may know (vv. 17-18)
parts.note: The prayer ends harshly, asking that the enemies be shamed and dismayed for good and perish in disgrace. Its stated aim is that they come to know the LORD alone is the Most High over all the earth, and readers differ on whether this hopes for their change of heart or simply for a defeat that proves who God is.

disagreement: Christians differ on how to read prayers like this for an enemy's ruin: some see them as a fair cry for God's justice against real violence, others as honest human anger later reshaped by Jesus' call to love enemies, and others apply them only to spiritual evil.
think: When someone threatens you or people you love, is there a difference between wanting them stopped and wanting them humiliated, and where do you tend to land?
